{{Short description|Convolution}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[category theory]], '''Day convolution''' is an operation on [[functor]]s that can be seen as a [[categorification|categorified]] version of [[convolution|function convolution]].  It was first introduced by Brian Day in 1970<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Day |first1=Brian |title=On closed categories of functors |journal=Reports of the Midwest Category Seminar IV, Lecture Notes in Mathematics |date=1970 |volume=139 |pages=1–38}}</ref> in the general context of [[Enriched category|enriched]] [[functor category|functor categories]]. 

Day convolution gives a [[symmetric monoidal category|symmetric monoidal]] structure on <math>\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})</math> for two symmetric monoidal categories <math>\mathbf{C}, \mathbf{D}</math>.

Another related version is that Day convolution acts as a tensor product for a [[monoidal category]] structure on the category of functors <math>[\mathbf{C},V]</math> over some [[monoidal category]] <math>V</math>.

== Definition ==

=== First version ===

Given <math>F,G \colon \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{D}</math> for two symmetric monoidal <math>\mathbf{C}, \mathbf{D}</math>, we define their Day convolution as follows.

It is the left [[kan extension]] along <math>\mathbf{C} \times \mathbf{C} \to^{\otimes} \mathbf{C}</math> of the composition <math>\mathbf{C} \times \mathbf{C} \to^{F,G} \mathbf{D} \times \mathbf{D} \to^{\otimes} \mathbf{D}</math>

Thus evaluated on an object <math>O \in \mathbf{C}</math>, intuitively we get a [[colimit]] in <math>\mathbf{D}</math> of <math>F(x) \otimes G(y)</math> along approximations of <math>O \in \mathbf{C}</math> as a pure tensor <math>x \otimes y</math>

Left kan extensions are computed via [[coend]]s, which leads to the version below.

=== Enriched version ===

Let <math>(\mathbf{C}, \otimes_c)</math> be a monoidal category enriched over a symmetric [[monoidal closed category]] <math>(V, \otimes)</math>. Given two functors <math>F,G \colon \mathbf{C} \to V</math>, we define their Day convolution as the following coend.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Loregian |first1=Fosco |title=(Co)end Calculus |chapter= |arxiv=1501.02503 |page=51|year=2021 |doi=10.1017/9781108778657 |isbn=9781108778657 |s2cid=237839003 }}</ref>

:<math>F \otimes_d G = \int^{x,y \in \mathbf{C}} \mathbf{C}(x \otimes_c y , -) \otimes Fx \otimes Gy</math>

If <math>\otimes_c</math> is symmetric, then <math>\otimes_d</math> is also symmetric. We can show this defines an associative monoidal product:

:<math>\begin{aligned} & (F \otimes_d G) \otimes_d H \\[5pt]
\cong {} & \int^{c_1,c_2} (F \otimes_d G)c_1 \otimes Hc_2 \otimes \mathbf{C}(c_1 \otimes_c c_2, -) \\[5pt]
\cong {} & \int^{c_1,c_2} \left( \int^{c_3,c_4} Fc_3 \otimes Gc_4 \otimes \mathbf{C}(c_3 \otimes_c c_4 , c_1) \right) \otimes Hc_2 \otimes \mathbf{C}(c_1 \otimes_c c_2, -) \\[5pt]
\cong {} & \int^{c_1,c_2,c_3,c_4} Fc_3 \otimes Gc_4 \otimes Hc_2 \otimes \mathbf{C}(c_3 \otimes_c c_4 , c_1) \otimes \mathbf{C}(c_1 \otimes_c c_2, -) \\[5pt]
\cong {} & \int^{c_1,c_2,c_3,c_4} Fc_3 \otimes Gc_4 \otimes Hc_2 \otimes \mathbf{C}(c_3 \otimes_c c_4 \otimes_c c_2, -)  \\[5pt]
\cong {} & \int^{c_1,c_2,c_3,c_4} Fc_3 \otimes Gc_4 \otimes Hc_2 \otimes \mathbf{C}(c_2 \otimes_c c_4 , c_1) \otimes \mathbf{C}(c_3 \otimes_c c_1, -) \\[5pt]
\cong {} & \int^{c_1,c_3} Fc_3 \otimes (G \otimes_d H)c_1 \otimes \mathbf{C}(c_3 \otimes_c c_1, -) \\[5pt]
\cong {} & F \otimes_d (G \otimes_d H)\end{aligned}</math>
